name: Hliðskjálf
powers: From it the sitter can see across all the worlds.
description: The high seat of Odin in Valhöll, from which the All-Father can see into all realms and watch over everything that happens among gods, men, and giants. Sitting in Hliðskjálf without leave was dangerous: Freyr sat in it and was struck by the sight of the giantess Gerðr, falling in love with her at a distance. It appears throughout the Eddas as the seat of far-seeing power.

name: Hringhorni
powers: The greatest of ships, large enough to bear a god's funeral pyre.
description: The greatest of all ships, in which the gods laid the body of Baldr upon a funeral pyre after his death by the mistletoe spear. The launching of Hringhorni was so heavy that only the giantess Hyrrokkin could push it into the sea. It appears in the Prose Edda's account of Baldr's funeral and in some skaldic references.

name: Hǫfuð
powers: The sword of Heimdall, watchman of the gods, named among his possessions in the Edda.
description: Hǫfuð, 'Head', the sword of Heimdall, watchman of the gods, named among his possessions in Gylfaginning. Snorri lists the blade beside Heimdall's role as guardian of the gods, and later tradition links it to the final battle, where Heimdall and Loki are said to slay each other at Ragnarök. It is one of the few named Eddic swords with no surviving owner story.

name: The Holy Spring
maker: Natural spring, named for a saint
powers: Healing water for the sick who visit on the appointed day.
description: The holy spring (heliga källan), a spring or well that Swedish folk tradition credited with healing. Such springs, often named for a saint, were visited for cures on particular days; pilgrims left offerings of coins, linen, or crosses, and some springs were said to swell or glow before miracles. Many Swedish holy springs became pilgrimage sites that the church later absorbed or closed.
source: Swedish holy-spring tradition and place-name studies

name: Hjortspring Boat
description: A slender light war canoe of linden wood, about 18 meters long, dug from a bog on the island of Als, Denmark, in 1921 along with the shields and spears of a defeated army. Built around 350 BCE, it held perhaps twenty paddlers and was offered up after battle, likely a sacrifice of the enemy's arms. It is the oldest and finest of the Nordic war boats and rests in the National Museum of Denmark.

name: Perseus' Sickle
powers: Could sever the head of Medusa and shear through stone and serpent.
description: The curved sickle-sword, harpe, with which Perseus beheaded the Gorgon Medusa, given to him by Hermes on his quest. Ancient sources describe it as a sword or sickle that could shear through stone and serpent, and the severed head's gaze still petrified his foes. It closes the Medusa episode and arms Athena with the gorgoneion.

name: Hermes’ Sandals
powers: Grants the wearer winged speed and the ability to travel instantly across realms.
description: The winged sandals of Hermes, the messenger god, enable swift travel and serve as a symbol of speed and cunning in Greek mythology.

name: Heian Court Fan
powers: Elegant signaling device; used in court dances and ceremonies.
description: A delicate folding fan employed by Heian courtiers to convey subtle messages and as an accessory in classical dances. Its painted motifs often depict seasonal scenes.

name: Hannya Mask
powers: Embodies a woman turned demon by jealousy
description: A Noh theatre mask sculpted as the face of a woman twisted by jealousy into a horned, serpent-eyed demon, with metal fangs and a grimacing mouth. Carried by performers in plays such as Dojoji and Aoi no Ue, the hannya shows obsession consuming the living into demonic form, and the mask itself is held to retain dangerous power.

name: Hagoromo
powers: Lets its wearer fly between heaven and earth
description: The feather mantle that lets a heavenly maiden (tennyo) fly between the mortal world and the sky. In the classic Noh play Hagoromo, a fisherman of Mio Bay finds one hung on a pine and makes the angel dance before returning it; the robe marks the tenuous boundary between human and divine realms in Japanese drama and folklore.
source: Noh play Hagoromo; coastal legend tradition

name: Hou Yi's Bow
powers: Shot down nine of the ten suns
description: The red bow of the legendary archer Hou Yi, who in Chinese myth shot down nine of the ten suns that scorched the earth, leaving one to light the day. His skill earned him the elixir of immortality, and his bow remains the emblem of marksmanship in tales of the heavenly archer and his doomed wife Chang'e.

name: The Heavenly Loom
powers: Wove the patterned clouds of the sky
description: The celestial loom of Zhinü, the Weaver Girl, who wove the patterned clouds of the sky beside the Heavenly River. When her marriage to the cowherd Niulang made her neglect her weaving, the Jade Emperor separated the pair, and on the seventh night of the seventh month magpies bridge the river for their yearly reunion, the origin of the Qixi festival.
source: Qixi legend; Han to Tang sources
